Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

PADUCAH, Kentucky (CNN) -- The aunt of former U.S. soldier Steven Green told jurors tearfully Monday that "We did not send a rapist and murderer to Iraq" as defense lawyers worked to save her nephew from a death sentence. Former U.S. soldier Steven Green has been convicted of raping and killing a 14-year-old Iraqi girl. Patty Ruth, a Texas elementary school principal, told a civilian jury about Green's childhood as a reader who loved to be hugged by relatives. "I do not know how we got to this spot," Ruth said in emotional testimony. "I do not know how this happened." Green was convicted last week in U.S. District Court in Kentucky of murder, rape, conspiracy and obstruction of justice in connection with a 2006 rape-and-murder south of Baghdad. A jury found him guilty of raping a 14-year-old girl, then killing her and setting her body on fire to destroy evidence. Green also was found guilty of killing the girl's parents and 6-year-old sister. He could become the first former U.S. soldier to face the death penalty for war crimes before a civilian court, where he was tried because he had been discharged from the military before his crimes came to light. Four other former soldiers are in prison for their roles in the crimes and the cover-up that followed. Green faces either death or life in prison without the possibility of parole. His fate will be in the hands of the jury by week's end. The defense has presented relatives and medical professionals who have pieced together a picture of Green's childhood as troubled and stressful. It included the breakup of his parents' marriage, routine beatings to the point of injury by an older brother and being moved about through Texas by his mother. Ruth, the final witness scheduled by the defense, said that when the idea of the military came up for her nephew, she was unsure the Army would accept him. Even after he received a high school diploma through a correspondence course, she said, "I could not picture or imagine how he could make it through basic training." Ruth said when she saw a picture of her nephew before his September 2005 deployment, she knew he wasn't "Stevie" anymore, standing as tall as his father in the photo at Fort Benning, Georgia. When he returned from Iraq 11 months later, he was "remarkably thin," Ruth said, and she noticed circles under his eyes. Green and his father spent a night at the Ruth home, his aunt said, and she remembered him pacing the yard while smoking. He fell asleep wearing his fatigues, she said. When asked by the defense about the rape-murder plot that left an Iraqi family dead near Yusufiya, about 20 miles south of Baghdad, Ruth responded, "He's my Steve. You can't stop loving someone." There were other family members in the court on Monday. Green's father, John, an oil field worker from Midland, Texas, looked on quietly. He did not testify. Ruth, who is John Green's sister, noted for the jury that Green's mother is not at the trial this week. The mother is moving and had to attend a going-away party, Ruth said. Final arguments are expected Wednesday.

Green has been convicted of raping and killing a 14-year-old Iraqi girl.

Patty Ruth, a Texas elementary school principal, described Green’s childhood to a civilian jury, recalling him as an avid reader who loved being hugged by relatives.

“I do not know how we got to this spot,” Ruth said during emotional testimony. “I do not know how this happened.”

Last week, Green was convicted in U.S. District Court in Kentucky of murder, rape, conspiracy and obstruction of justice in connection with a 2006 rape and murder south of Baghdad. A jury found him guilty of raping the 14-year-old girl, killing her and setting her body on fire to destroy evidence. He was also found guilty of killing the girl’s parents and 6-year-old sister.

Green could become the first former U.S. soldier to face the death penalty for war crimes in a civilian court. He was tried there because he had been discharged from the military before his crimes came to light.

Four other former soldiers are serving prison sentences for their roles in the crimes and the subsequent cover-up.

Green faces either death or life in prison without the possibility of parole. His fate is expected to be in the jury’s hands by the end of the week.

The defense has called relatives and medical professionals who have portrayed Green’s childhood as troubled and stressful. His early life included the breakup of his parents’ marriage, routine beatings by an older brother that left him injured, and frequent moves across Texas with his mother.

Ruth, the defense’s final scheduled witness, said she had been uncertain whether the Army would accept her nephew when the possibility of military service arose. Even after he earned a high school diploma through a correspondence course, she said, “I could not picture or imagine how he could make it through basic training.”

Ruth said that when she saw a photograph of her nephew before his September 2005 deployment, she realized he was no longer “Stevie.” In the photograph, taken at Fort Benning, Georgia, he stood as tall as his father.

When Green returned from Iraq 11 months later, he was “remarkably thin,” Ruth said, and she noticed circles beneath his eyes.

Green and his father spent a night at Ruth’s home, she said. She recalled Green pacing the yard while smoking and later falling asleep in his fatigues.

When defense attorneys asked her about the rape and murder plot that left an Iraqi family dead near Yusufiya, about 20 miles south of Baghdad, Ruth replied, “He’s my Steve. You can’t stop loving someone.”

Other family members were in court Monday. Green’s father, John, an oil field worker from Midland, Texas, watched quietly but did not testify.

Ruth, John Green’s sister, told the jury that Green’s mother was not attending the trial this week because she was moving and had to attend a going-away party.

Closing arguments are expected Wednesday.

PADUCAH, Kentucky (CNN) — As Steven Green’s attorneys sought to prevent jurors from sentencing him to death, his aunt broke down in tears Monday and insisted that the family had not sent “a rapist and murderer to Iraq.”

Green, a former U.S. soldier, was found guilty of raping and murdering a 14-year-old Iraqi girl. His aunt, Patty Ruth, an elementary school principal in Texas, described him to the civilian jury as a child who enjoyed reading and receiving hugs from family members.

“I do not know how we got to this spot,” Ruth testified emotionally. “I do not know how this happened.”

The previous week, a federal jury in Kentucky convicted Green of murder, rape, conspiracy and obstruction of justice for his involvement in a 2006 rape and multiple killings south of Baghdad. Jurors concluded that he raped the teenage girl, murdered her and burned her body in an effort to eliminate evidence. He was also convicted of killing her parents and her 6-year-old sister.

Because Green had left the military before the crimes were discovered, his case was heard in civilian court. He could become the first former American service member sentenced to death by a civilian court for war crimes. Four other former soldiers are serving prison terms for taking part in the offenses and the subsequent cover-up.

The jury must choose between execution and life imprisonment without parole. A decision was expected by the end of the week.

To support their request for leniency, Green’s defense lawyers called relatives and medical experts who portrayed his upbringing as difficult and unstable. His parents’ marriage ended, an older brother regularly beat him severely enough to cause injuries, and his mother repeatedly moved him around Texas.

Ruth, the defense’s last scheduled witness, said she doubted the Army would take her nephew when military service was first discussed. Although he earned a high school diploma through a correspondence program, she said, “I could not picture or imagine how he could make it through basic training.”

After seeing a photograph taken before Green deployed in September 2005, Ruth said she realized he was no longer “Stevie.” In the picture from Fort Benning, Georgia, he stood as tall as his father.

When Green came home from Iraq 11 months later, Ruth recalled that he was “remarkably thin” and had dark circles beneath his eyes. He and his father stayed one night at her house, where she saw Green smoke while walking back and forth across the yard. She said he eventually fell asleep still dressed in his military fatigues.

Asked by defense attorneys about the plan to rape and kill that resulted in the deaths of the Iraqi family near Yusufiya, approximately 20 miles south of Baghdad, Ruth replied, “He’s my Steve. You can’t stop loving someone.”

Other relatives attended Monday’s court proceedings. Green’s father, John Green, an oil-field worker from Midland, Texas, watched silently and did not take the witness stand. Ruth, John Green’s sister, also pointed out that Green’s mother was absent from the trial that week because she was moving and needed to attend a farewell party.

Closing arguments were expected Wednesday.

Green was convicted of raping 14-year-old Abeer Qassim al-Janabi and killing her, her parents and her 6-year-old sister at their home near Mahmoudiya, Iraq, in March 2006. Defense lawyers did not dispute the gravity of the crimes. Instead, they urged jurors to impose life in prison without parole, arguing that Green’s chaotic upbringing and the psychological strain surrounding his deployment helped explain how he reached the point of committing the offenses. They also pointed to failures in military supervision and discipline.

Prosecutors argued that the killings were deliberate and methodical, telling jurors that Green made choices at every stage of the attack and then participated in efforts to cover it up. They said the victims’ vulnerability and the brutality of the crimes justified a death sentence.

Green, who had been discharged from the Army before the allegations emerged, was tried in civilian court under a federal law allowing the United States to prosecute certain crimes committed overseas by former service members.

The sentencing decision required a unanimous jury. Without unanimity for death, Green would receive life in federal prison without the possibility of release.

# ‘We Did Not Send a Rapist and Murderer to Iraq’: Why Steven Green Faced Execution

**PADUCAH, Ky. —** “We did not send a rapist and murderer to Iraq.”

The blunt declaration came from **Assistant U.S. Attorney Brian Skaret**, one of the federal prosecutors in the case against former Army private **Steven Dale Green**. It was intended to reject the defense’s central effort to portray Green as a damaged young soldier whose crimes were the product of a brutal deployment, poor leadership and the psychological pressures of war.

Prosecutors argued that Green had not simply been swept along by combat. He had made a series of deliberate choices that culminated in one of the most notorious atrocities committed by American troops during the Iraq War: the rape of an Iraqi girl and the murder of her and three members of her family.

A federal jury in Kentucky convicted Green in May 2009 for his role in the March 12, 2006, attack near **Mahmudiyah**, south of Baghdad. Prosecutors said Green and several other soldiers planned the assault while drinking alcohol and playing cards at a checkpoint.

The soldiers went to the home of **Abeer Qassim Hamza al-Janabi**, who was 14, according to Iraqi records and the federal indictment. Green shot and killed her father, mother and six-year-old sister, prosecutors said. He and another soldier raped Abeer before Green shot her in the head. The soldiers then attempted to burn her body and clothing to conceal the crime.

The killings initially appeared to be the work of insurgents. The truth emerged months later after a soldier disclosed details of the attack.

## A civilian prosecution of a former soldier

Green’s case differed from those of the other soldiers involved because he had already been discharged from the Army before investigators identified him as a suspect. The military had sent him home with a personality-disorder discharge, meaning he was no longer subject to an ordinary court-martial when the crime was uncovered.

Federal prosecutors instead charged him under the **Military Extraterritorial Jurisdiction Act**, which permits the United States to prosecute certain crimes committed overseas by members of the armed forces and other people connected to military operations.

Because Green was arrested and brought into the civilian federal court system, his trial took place in western Kentucky, where he had been living after leaving the Army. The Justice Department authorized prosecutors to seek the death penalty.

Green was convicted of offenses including murder, aggravated sexual abuse and conspiracy. Several of the murder counts were capital offenses under federal law, allowing the same jury to decide whether he should be executed.

That possibility did not depend on Kentucky’s death-penalty law. Green was prosecuted under **federal law**, and federal capital punishment could be sought even though the crimes occurred outside the United States.

## Prosecutors: War did not excuse the choices

At trial, Green’s lawyers did not seriously dispute that he had participated in the attack. Instead, they emphasized his youth, psychological problems, alcohol use and the conditions faced by his unit in Iraq.

His platoon had suffered casualties, endured long hours at exposed checkpoints and operated in a violent area with insufficient supervision, the defense said. Green, who was 20 at the time of the killings, had voiced hostility toward Iraqis and showed signs of emotional deterioration before the attack.

Defense lawyers argued that Army commanders had ignored warning signs and had deployed or retained a soldier who was poorly suited to combat. During the penalty phase, they urged jurors to consider whether failures in recruitment, screening, discipline and mental-health care had helped create the circumstances in which the crime occurred.

Skaret’s statement — “We did not send a rapist and murderer to Iraq” — was the prosecution’s answer to that argument. The government maintained that military stress could not account for the planning involved: changing clothes to avoid detection, approaching the family’s house, separating Abeer from her relatives, killing the witnesses and trying to burn the evidence.

The prosecution’s position was that Green had personal agency and should not be permitted to shift responsibility to the Army or the war.

## Why the death penalty was available

Under federal law, a jury may impose a death sentence for specified murders if prosecutors prove the required aggravating factors beyond a reasonable doubt. In Green’s case, the government argued that the murders were especially grave because several people were killed, a child was among the victims, the killings occurred during a sexual assault and the family was targeted as part of a planned criminal act.

The sentencing process required two stages. After determining Green’s guilt, jurors heard additional evidence about whether he should be executed. Prosecutors presented the brutality of the crime and its impact. Defense lawyers offered mitigating evidence about Green’s background, mental health, age and military service.

A federal death sentence had to be **unanimous**. If even one juror refused to vote for execution, the court could not impose it.

That requirement ultimately spared Green’s life. The jury failed to reach a unanimous death verdict, resulting in a sentence of **life in prison without the possibility of release**. In September 2009, a federal judge formally sentenced him to five consecutive life terms.

Green later died in federal custody in 2014 after an apparent suicide.

## Other soldiers received prison terms

The other soldiers implicated in the attack remained in military jurisdiction and were prosecuted in courts-martial after agreeing to plea deals or being convicted.

**James Barker**, **Paul Cortez**, **Jesse Spielman** and **Bryan Howard** received prison sentences of varying lengths for their roles in the crime and its planning or concealment. Barker and Cortez testified against Green, describing the preparation for the assault and Green’s actions inside the house.

Their testimony helped prosecutors establish that the attack was not a spontaneous battlefield encounter. The family was unarmed, the home posed no military threat, and the soldiers left their post intending to commit the crime.

The case became a stark test of whether U.S. law could reach a former service member accused of atrocities committed abroad. It also exposed failures within the military unit and intensified debate over combat stress, discipline and command responsibility.

But for prosecutors, those wider failures did not erase individual guilt. Skaret’s line captured the government’s case in a single sentence: the Army may have placed Green in Iraq, but, prosecutors argued, Green himself chose to rape and kill.

counterfactuals.output:
**PADUCAH, Ky., May 2009 —** The federal trial of former U.S. soldier Steven Dale Green entered its penalty phase after a jury convicted him of raping 14-year-old Abeer Qassim Hamza al-Janabi and murdering her and three members of her family near Yusufiya, Iraq, in March 2006.

Relatives testified from Iraq, largely through video links or recorded depositions, about the family’s loss. Abeer’s surviving brothers described returning from school to learn that their parents, younger sister and Abeer had been killed. They told jurors that the deaths left them dependent on relatives, disrupted their schooling and continued to cause fear, grief and social stigma. Other family members described having to care for the orphaned boys and the lasting emotional and financial consequences of the killings.

Prosecutors argued that the calculated nature of the attack—including separating Abeer from her family, killing the others, raping and shooting her, and trying to burn her body—justified execution. Green’s lawyers planned extensive mitigation testimony about his troubled upbringing, mental health, drug and alcohol abuse, and the pressures and failures surrounding his Army deployment.

The penalty hearing was expected to last roughly two weeks, with the defense presenting dozens of witnesses after the government finished its case. The same jury would then decide between death and life imprisonment without parole. A death sentence required a unanimous verdict; absent unanimity, Green would receive life. The jury ultimately failed to agree on death, and Green was later sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of release.
